title: Facet primes and normalized monomial valuations of complete toric models
statement:
Let $P$ be a finitely generated integral saturated commutative monoid [def-trf-fs-log-blowup], written additively, and suppose it is sharp, meaning that $0$ is its only invertible element. Let $n\geq0$ be an integer. For a coefficient ring $L$, write $L[P][t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ for the ring of finite sums of symbols $c z^q t^e$, with $q\in P$, $e\in\mathbf N^n$, $c\in L$, and multiplication $z^qz^{q'}=z^{q+q'}$. If $L$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_L$, let $B_L(P,n)$ be its completion [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] at $(\mathfrak m_L,z^q\ (q
eq0),t_1,\ldots,t_n)$. Let $R$ be one of the following rings: (i) $B_k(P,n)$ for a field $k$; (ii) $B_C(P,n)/(	heta)$ for a Cohen ring $C$ of residue characteristic $p$ [def-weil-pbc-cohen-ring] and $	heta-p\in(z^q\ (q
eq0),t_1,\ldots,t_n)B_C(P,n)$. In case (ii), $p$ is prime and the residue field of $C$ is arbitrary of characteristic $p$. Write $z^q$ for the chart monomials in $R$. Assume $R$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Put $G=P^{m gp}$, let $V=G\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, and let $\sigma\subset V$ be the cone of nonnegative rational linear combinations of the images of $P$. A facet is a face of $\sigma$ of codimension one; explicitly it is a subset $F=\sigma\cap\ker h$, for a nonzero rational linear form $h:V	o\mathbf Q$ nonnegative on $\sigma$, with $\dim F=\dim V-1$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of facets. Then $R$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and every $z^q$ is nonzero. The set $\mathcal F$ is finite, and for each $F\in\mathcal F$ there is a unique homomorphism $
u_F:G	o\mathbf Z$ nonnegative on $P$, with image $\mathbf Z$ and $F=\sigma\cap\ker
u_F$. These forms satisfy
$$\sigma=\{v\in V:
u_F(v)\geq0	ext{ for all }F\in\mathcal F\},$$
where each $
u_F$ is extended rationally to $V$. The ideals
$$\mathfrak p_F=(z^q:q\in P,\ q
otin F)R$$
are distinct height-one prime ideals, and they are exactly the height-one prime ideals of $R$ containing at least one chart monomial $z^q$. Height one means that the prime is nonzero and no prime lies strictly between it and $(0)$. The local ring $R_{\mathfrak p_F}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Its normalized additive valuation $v_F:\operatorname{Frac}(R)^	imes	o\mathbf Z$ (a uniformizer has value one) satisfies
$$v_F(z^q)=
u_F(q)\qquad(q\in P).$$
For $P=\{0\}$ the facet set and the list of boundary primes are empty, and the displayed half-space intersection is $V=0$.

source.place: Boundary-prime and valuation input to the complete-local recognition equality, replacing the unsupported converse application of VI 1.6. ILO VI 1.4 and 1.6, printed pp. 69--70, motivate the model and the recognition problem; they do not state or prove this auxiliary theorem. Agent-formulated algebraic input for the direct divisor route. Kato (1994), Toric singularities, especially Theorem 11.6, is WANTED for the underlying toric divisor theory; no proof is attributed to an unread source.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-sharp-cone-lattice-intersection] to $P$. It gives a finite free lattice $G\subset V$, a finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in P$ generating $\sigma$ rationally, pointedness and spanning of $\sigma$, and $P=\sigma\cap G$. If $G=0$, then $P=\{0\}$ and $V=\sigma=0$, so the facet assertions hold with an empty set. For the cone argument in Steps 2--5 suppose $d=\dim V>0$.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-rational-cone-dual-finite], $\sigma$ is the nonnegative locus of a finite rational family $h_i$. Delete zero forms and successively delete redundant inequalities, stopping with an irredundant family indexed by a finite set $I$. Each remaining $h_i$ is nonzero and nonnegative on $P$. Put $x_0=\sum_j a_j$. Then $h_i(x_0)>0$ for every $i$: otherwise nonnegativity forces $h_i(a_j)=0$ for every generator, and spanning forces $h_i=0$. Thus $x_0$ is a rational point satisfying all inequalities strictly. The family is nonempty when $d>0$, since otherwise $\sigma=V$ would contradict pointedness.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text:
For each $i\in I$, irredundancy supplies $y_i\in V$ satisfying $h_j(y_i)\ge0$ for $j
e i$ and $h_i(y_i)<0$. On the rational segment from $x_0$ to $y_i$, let $f_i$ be the unique point with $h_i(f_i)=0$. The coefficient of $x_0$ is strictly positive, so $h_j(f_i)>0$ for every $j
e i$. Choose a basis $u_1,\ldots,u_{d-1}$ of $\ker h_i$. For each $u_l$, choose rational $\epsilon_l>0$ with $\epsilon_l|h_j(u_l)|<h_j(f_i)$ whenever $j
e i$ and $h_j(u_l)
e0$. Then $f_i+\epsilon_l u_l$ still satisfies all inequalities. Differences from $f_i$ span $\ker h_i$, showing that $F_i=\sigma\cap\ker h_i$ spans $\ker h_i$, hence is a facet. Moreover $f_i
otin F_j$ for $j
e i$, so these facets are distinct.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text: Conversely take any facet $F=\sigma\cap\ker h$, with $h\ge0$ on $\sigma$. In a nonnegative generator expression for a point of $F$, every occurring $a_j$ has $h(a_j)=0$. Thus these zero-valued generators generate $F$ as a rational cone. Let $a$ be their sum, with the empty sum allowed. At least one $h_i(a)$ is zero: if all were positive, choose $v\in V$ with $h(v)<0$ and rational $\epsilon>0$ with $\epsilon|h_i(v)|<h_i(a)$ for each nonzero $h_i(v)$. Then every $h_i(a+\epsilon v)>0$, so $a+\epsilon v\in\sigma$, whereas $h(a+\epsilon v)=\epsilon h(v)<0$, a contradiction. Nonnegativity of $h_i$ on the zero-valued generators and $h_i(a)=0$ imply that $h_i$ vanishes on all of $F$. Since $F$ spans a hyperplane, $\ker h_i=\operatorname{span}F=\ker h$, and $F=F_i$. This proves that the finite list in Step 3 is exactly $\mathcal F$, and that its supporting inequalities still cut out $\sigma$.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text:
For $F_i$, clear the rational denominators of $h_i$ on a finite $\mathbf Z$-basis of $G$, then divide the resulting integer coordinates by their positive gcd. This gives $
u_{F_i}:G	o\mathbf Z$ with image $\mathbf Z$ and a positive rational multiple of $h_i$ as rational extension. Its sign and zero locus are unchanged, so these primitive forms cut out $\sigma$. If another primitive nonnegative form defines $F_i$, it has the same hyperplane kernel, hence is $c
u_{F_i}$ for $c\in\mathbf Q_{>0}$. The two image conditions give $c\mathbf Z=\mathbf Z$, so $c=1$. Finally multiply the rational $f_i$ of Step 3 by a positive integer so that $f_i\in G$. It then belongs to $P$ by Step 1, with $
u_{F_i}(f_i)=0$ and $
u_H(f_i)>0$ for all other facets $H$. For a sole rank-one facet one may take $f_i=0$.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text: The coefficient ring $L$ is Noetherian: a field has only two ideals; a Cohen ring is a principal ideal domain by [def-weil-pbc-cohen-ring]. If $g_1,\ldots,g_s$ generate $P$, the map $L[X_1,\ldots,X_s,t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to L[P][t]$ sending $X_i$ to $z^{g_i}$ is surjective. Hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] makes the monoid polynomial ring Noetherian, [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-noetherian] makes $B_L(P,n)$ Noetherian, and [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-image-noetherian] gives the same for its quotient $R$ in case (ii).

By [lem-trf-sharp-monoid-positive-grading], choose $w:G\to\mathbf Z$ positive on $P\setminus\{0\}$. Put $T=P\times\mathbf N^n\subset G\times\mathbf Z^n$ and $W(q,e)=w(q)+\sum e_i$, positive on $T\setminus\{0\}$. The coefficient ring is complete separated local (trivially for a field, by [def-weil-pbc-cohen-ring] for $C$). Apply [lem-trf-monoid-completion-coefficients] to $L,T,W$. Relabelling $z^{(q,e)}$ as $z^qt^e$ identifies its completion with $B_L(P,n)$, and identifies its elements with all $L$-coefficient families on $T$, with finite convolution. In particular $z^q$ is nonzero in case (i).

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text: In case (ii), $\theta$ has constant coefficient $p$: the other generators of the stipulated ideal have positive $W$-weight, so any multiple has zero constant coefficient. If $z^q=\theta b$ before quotienting, induct on the integer weight of exponents $u$ below $W(q,0)$. At such a $u$ the convolution equation is $0=p b_u$ plus terms involving only $b_v$ of smaller weight. Induction and the fact that $p\ne0$ in the domain $C$ give $b_u=0$ for all those exponents. The coefficient equation at $(q,0)$ is then $1=p b_{(q,0)}$, impossible because $p$ is a nonunit. Thus no $z^q$ lies in $(\theta)$, including $q=0$. This proves monomial nonvanishing in $R$ without appealing to a construction in another node's proof.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text: Fix a facet $F$ and put $S=P\cap F$. This is a face of $P$: $\nu_F(a+b)=0$ with $a,b\in P$ forces both nonnegative summands to be zero. In a generator expression for an element of $S$, every occurring $g_i$ therefore lies in $S$; thus $S$ is generated by the subset of the $g_i$ in $F$. Integrality and sharpness are inherited from $P$. For saturation, if $N g\in S$ for $g\in S^{\rm gp}\subset G$ and $N>0$, saturation of $P$ gives $g\in P$, and $N\nu_F(g)=0$ gives $g\in S$. Consequently $S$ is also sharp fs. The weight $w$ restricts positively to $S$, so the coefficient description of Step 7 applies to $S\times\mathbf N^n$ as well.

source.place: Agent-written algebraic argument for the complete models displayed in Expose VI 1.6, printed p. 70; not an assertion that ILO proves this step.

proof.text:
On coefficient families, keep precisely the exponents $(q,e)$ with $q\in S$. This defines a surjective ring map $ho:B_L(P,n)	o B_L(S,n)$: for an exponent in $S$, the face property forces both exponents in every convolution summand to be in $S$, and extension by zero gives surjectivity. Its kernel is the ideal generated by the finitely many $z^{g_i}$ with $g_i
otin F$. Indeed every exponent $q
otin F$ is divisible by one such generator. Assign each such $q$ to one choice of $g_i$, and form the family $b_i$ by moving its assigned coefficient at $(q,e)$ to $(q-g_i,e)$. The coefficient lemma allows every such family. Thus every element of the kernel equals the finite sum $\sum_{g_i
otin F}z^{g_i}b_i$. Conversely each summand has support outside $S$. This also proves that this ideal is generated by all $z^q$ with $q
otin F$.

proof.text: In case (i), Step 10 gives $R/\mathfrak p_F\cong B_k(S,n)$. In case (ii), let $\theta_S=\rho(\theta)$. It still satisfies $\theta_S-p\in(z^s:s\in S\setminus\{0\},t_1,\ldots,t_n)$, and the surjectivity and kernel calculation give $R/\mathfrak p_F\cong B_C(S,n)/(\theta_S)$. Apply [lem-trf-log-regular-saturation-normality] to the sharp fs monoid $S$ and this unchanged coefficient alternative. Its statement says that each of these quotient models is a nonzero normal domain. Hence $\mathfrak p_F$ is prime. The coefficient and weight argument in Steps 7--8, now for $S$, shows that all its chart monomials are nonzero. In particular, a monomial $z^q$ lies in $\mathfrak p_F$ if and only if $q\notin F$.

For $F
e H$, the lattice point $f_F$ constructed in Step 5 lies in $F$ and not in $H$. Thus $z^{f_F}
otin\mathfrak p_F$ but $z^{f_F}\in\mathfrak p_H$, proving distinctness. Also each $\mathfrak p_F$ is nonzero: the nonzero $
u_F$ takes a positive value on some generator of $P$ since $P$ spans $V$, and its nonzero monomial lies in $\mathfrak p_F$. Put $A_F=R_{\mathfrak p_F}$. By [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak p_FA_F$. It is a Noetherian domain: it embeds in $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, and any ideal of $A_F$ is generated by images of generators of its contraction to $R$, because denominators are units.

Choose $e\in G$ with $
u_F(e)=1$, possible by primitivity. For the lattice point $f=f_F\in P\cap F$ of Step 5, all other facet values are strictly positive. Choose $N\ge0$ so that $
u_H(e)+N
u_H(f)\ge0$ for all $H
e F$. Then $e+Nf\in\sigma\cap G=P$, whereas $Nf\in P\cap F$. In $A_F$ define $\pi=z^{e+Nf}/z^{Nf}$. Its denominator is outside $\mathfrak p_F$ by Step 11, its numerator is in $\mathfrak p_F$, and both monomials are nonzero, so $\pi$ is a nonzero element of the maximal ideal.

For $q\in P$ write $m=
u_F(q)\ge0$ and $g=q-me\in\ker
u_F$. Choose $M\ge0$ so that $
u_H(g)+M
u_H(f)\ge0$ for all $H
e F$. The half-space equality and $P=\sigma\cap G$ give $g+Mf\in P\cap F$. Consequently $u_q=z^{g+Mf}/z^{Mf}$ is a unit of $A_F$. Cancellation of the nonzero monomials in the fraction field gives $z^q=u_q\pi^m$. In particular every generator $z^{g_i}$ of $\mathfrak p_F$ is divisible by $\pi$ in $A_F$, since its value $
u_F(g_i)>0$. Step 13 already put $\pi$ in that ideal, so $\mathfrak p_FA_F=(\pi)$. This gives a generator, rather than assuming that a primitive lattice character is a uniformizer.

proof.text: The ring $A_F$ is a Noetherian local domain with maximal ideal generated by the single nonzero element $\pi$. The equivalent characterization in [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] therefore makes it a DVR. To check the stipulated height-one convention explicitly, [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-local-dimension-le-generators] gives $\dim A_F\le1$. Its nonzero maximal ideal supplies a chain $(0)\subsetneq(\pi)$, so its dimension is one. Primes of $R$ contained in $\mathfrak p_F$ correspond by extension and contraction to primes of $A_F$: denominators avoid all these primes, so contraction of an extension recovers the original prime, and a fraction belongs to an extended ideal exactly when its numerator does. Hence no prime of $R$ lies strictly between $(0)$ and $\mathfrak p_F$, which is the required height-one assertion.

The fraction field of $A_F$ is $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, since $R\subset A_F\subset\operatorname{Frac}(R)$. Let $v_F$ be its normalized additive valuation. By [lem-sc-dvr-valuation-ring-characterization], $v_F(\pi)=1$ and the values of a unit $u$ and $u^{-1}$ are both nonnegative. By [lem-sc-dvr-valuation-arithmetic] their sum is $v_F(1)=0$, so a unit has value zero. Apply the same additivity to the equality $z^q=u_q\pi^{\nu_F(q)}$ proved in Step 14. It gives $v_F(z^q)=\nu_F(q)$, including $q=0$.

proof.text:
Let $\mathfrak q$ be a height-one prime containing a monomial $z^a$. Suppose that no $\mathfrak p_F$ is contained in $\mathfrak q$. Since $\mathfrak p_F$ is generated by its monomials, for every $F$ choose $b_F\in P\setminus F$ with $z^{b_F}
otin\mathfrak q$. Set $b=\sum_F b_F$. Primality gives $z^b
otin\mathfrak q$, and for every facet $H$, $
u_H(b)\ge
u_H(b_H)>0$. Thus for a sufficiently large integer $K$, all $
u_H(Kb-a)\ge0$. The half-space identity and saturation equality $P=\sigma\cap G$ imply $Kb-a\in P$. But then $(z^b)^K=z^a z^{Kb-a}\in\mathfrak q$, contradicting primality. Therefore some $\mathfrak p_F\subseteq\mathfrak q$, and the nonzero prime $\mathfrak p_F$ and height-one convention force equality. Each $\mathfrak p_F$ itself contains a monomial by Step 12, proving both directions of the classification.

proof.text: If $P=\{0\}$, Step 1 gives $V=0$ and no facets. Its only chart monomial is $z^0=1$, which belongs to no prime, so the boundary-prime list is empty. Steps 6--8 still prove Noetherianity and monomial nonvanishing, and the empty half-space intersection in $V=0$ is $V$. For $n=0$, the product monoid in Step 7 is just $P$; no other step uses a parameter variable. This completes every clause, including the degenerate cases.

split_report.summary: Repaired D1 by dropping the two uncommitted clause-alias children and proving the item in 18 explicit steps using existing generic DAG inputs.
